title: Do you have to replace your helpdesk to use an AI agent?
summary: You can evaluate AI alongside an existing helpdesk. Check integrations, case ownership, reporting and handovers before assuming the current workflow will stay intact.
body_markdown:
Published October 6, 2026 · Updated October 15, 2026


You do not necessarily have to replace your helpdesk to introduce an AI agent. You can evaluate a setup that handles selected requests alongside it and returns the rest to your support team. Whether that works with your current desk depends on the integration, record keeping, permissions and handover you can actually test.


Separate the automation decision from the helpdesk replacement decision. That makes it easier to see what you want to preserve and what the AI should take on.


## Keep the operation you still depend on


In a September 2026 discussion, one of our cruise-industry customers described a concern about a possible Typewise AI-agent pilot. Several departments had moved onto its existing helpdesk, and the service team could not simply decide to replace it for everyone.


When a colleague explained the proposed alongside-the-helpdesk approach, the customer's service lead said he had understood the choice as either/or. The discussion changed how he viewed the project. It did not prove that the integration was complete or that the proposed automation had delivered a result.


Start your own review by listing what is built on the helpdesk: queues, case history, forms, knowledge pages, routing rules, reporting and access controls. Decide which functions must stay and which, if any, you intend to move. Do not assume "connects to the helpdesk" means all of them remain intact automatically.


## Follow one request through both systems


Ask the implementation team to show a normal request and an exception from arrival to completion. Check where the customer record lives, which system owns the case and what each system is allowed to change.


If the AI completes a request, determine what record the helpdesk needs for history and reporting. If it cannot complete it, check that the receiving support team gets the customer's question, relevant context and any actions already attempted. The original case identity should survive the transfer rather than leaving two unrelated tickets.


Test a customer replying after the handover. Which system receives the message? Can both respond by mistake?


Who owns the next step? Our guide to[AI handoff ownership](https://www.typewise.app/blog/ai-human-handoff-ownership) covers that waiting period and acceptance.


## Check the reporting you need to keep


Decide where you will measure total demand, human handling and AI outcomes. If completed AI cases never reach the helpdesk, its ticket count may no longer describe the whole service.


Keep fully automated resolution separate from drafts that people approve and cases where people perform a step. Check whether your existing reports can include those distinctions or need an explicitly agreed companion report. The[resolution guide](https://www.typewise.app/blog/ai-resolution-metrics-repeat-contacts) provides definitions you can use for that discussion.


The same applies to access and retention. Information copied into a second system needs appropriate permissions and a defined lifetime. A successful message transfer is not proof that those requirements are met.


## Start with the scope you can support


Pick a request type with usable data, clear action permissions and an available receiving team. Test the integration before sending live traffic, then use a supervised pilot to check the customer experience and remaining human effort.


The cruise customer's discussion also included practical dependencies and policy limits. The lesson is not that adding AI leaves every team's work unchanged. It is that you can investigate a bounded addition without committing to replace the whole helpdesk.


If you do not have a helpdesk, you still need somewhere to track unresolved cases and assign them to people. That might be an existing partner's system or another suitable tool. Evaluate that operating need separately from the choice of AI.


Write down one request you want the AI to handle and the helpdesk functions that must remain. Use that as the starting scope for a[go-live plan](https://www.typewise.app/blog/how-support-teams-go-live-with-ai) , including how you will pause the AI and return work to the normal queue.
